claims.status_note: #8, #13 and #29 describe the same overload and nobody disputes it. #21 disputes what counts as a bad report (c23), not the overload.
claims.text: The earlier bug bounty program was overwhelmed by false-positive and AI-generated slop submissions, and AI makes both finding critical bugs and filing spam reports cheap.

claims.status_note: #6 replies about who should fund bounties and how CHG should think about them, but nobody disputes or confirms that CHG is ill-equipped.
claims.text: Coinholder Grants (CHG) is ill-equipped to evaluate bounty requests beyond the very obvious Orchard soundness bug, and spam from earlier bounty programs is overflowing into it.

claims.status_note: #2, #8 and #31 argue it keeps out honest researchers (c5), and #5 defends it. thowar2 later says he is being convinced a bounty program may not be a good idea (#9), while #29 and #30 still back a fee.
claims.text: Requiring submitters to put up a bond or fee, forfeited if the report is rejected, raises the cost of slop above its payoff and deters it, while submitters confident in their finding will accept the risk.

claims.status_note: #4 argues he is a bad example and #2 says he reported because he is a board member. #6 and #15 restate the example without answering those points.
claims.text: Taylor Hornby's Orchard soundness report is a clear example of an existential finding that deserves a bounty, and reporters like him are who a program should reward.

claims.status_note: #5 answers #2 that a bond opens the doors to real reviewers rather than gatekeeping. #8 and #31 repeat the barrier concern and no one concedes.
claims.text: A bond or entry fee gatekeeps vulnerability reporting and prices out independent and good-faith researchers; a bounty should make reporting as attractive and hassle-free as possible so that bugs are not missed.

claims.status_note: #5 says ZF and ZCG already had multiple reviewers who were effectively DDOSed, which #7 answers by saying they were ordinary engineers with other duties. #9 prefers hiring bug hunters over reviewers, and #22 rejects that.
claims.text: Bug reports should be reviewed by dedicated, paid triagers or reviewers (full-time, part-time or on retainer) rather than by engineers on top of their existing duties.

claims.status_note: Nobody answers #4's points directly; #6 and #15 later continue to use him as an example without addressing them.
claims.text: Taylor Hornby is not representative of bounty finders: he reported as a paid auditor and board member, and a coinholder grant on top of an audit fee is not equivalent to a tiered, contractual bug bounty.

claims.status_note: #6 says coinholder votes should never be restricted by rules and exist to override exceptions, though norms are fine. #10 and #11 agree with the guard rails.
claims.text: Retroactive Grants need guard rails (no projects already declined by ZCG or FPF, no bug bounties unless network-breaking), and a real bounty program belongs in a separate system with set-aside funding and qualified reviewers.

claims.status_note: #7 says the earlier reviewers were not dedicated triagers. #26 says it is not an economic attack because nobody is paid before maintainers endorse a bug, and thowar2 does not reply.
claims.text: Flooding a bounty program with near-free fake or AI-generated reports is an asymmetric economic attack: ZF and ZCG reviewers were effectively DDOSed, and no system survives it unless the economics change.

claims.status_note: #30 gives a bounty that drew only about 300 submissions, #28 calls a bounty a huge net positive, and #26 says triagers handle the load. #9 states the view only tentatively; #33 states it firmly.
claims.text: Any formal bounty program will be gamed endlessly and is a waste of administrative effort, so the default should be no bounty program.

claims.status_note: #7 says one of his two reports was not practical but the other was fully exploitable and patched, and links an issue. The report itself is outside this thread, so it cannot be checked here.
claims.text: A bug report that strahncryptography posted publicly on another thread was disclosed irresponsibly and was not an exploitable bug.

claims.status_note: #22 says hiring bug hunters would be even worse than the alternatives and wants a full-time triager; the author of #9 does not return to the point.
claims.text: Funds are better spent hiring full-time bug hunters than hiring reviewers.

claims.status_note: #32 reports that critical vulnerabilities did receive payouts in the Q3 coinholder vote and #33 confirms. No post argues against discretionary payouts.
claims.text: Coinholders should vote discretionary bonus payouts, with no formal guarantee, only for truly existential bugs and reject most bounty requests, so they can judge rewards without committing funds to people gaming the system.

claims.status_note: #15 replies 'I don't disagree'; no evidence is linked and nobody disputes it.
claims.text: Many security researchers besides Taylor Hornby caught critical bugs, preventing issues like double spends and chain halts.

claims.status_note: #14 argues platform terms conflict with Zcash, and #22 rejects platforms. #17 finds a platform appealing but the 1 USDC fee too low.
claims.text: A bounty platform such as Immunefi, with spam filtering, PoC requirements, AI triage and a 1 USDC submission fee, is one of two workable options for a sustainable program, the other being a dedicated triager.

claims.status_note: #16 calls it another argument against any bounty program. Nobody disputes the terms-of-service point.
claims.text: Bounty platforms are unsuitable for Zcash: their terms of service conflict with its philosophy of shielded ZEC payouts, are often exclusionary, and risk legal battles and law-enforcement requests.

claims.status_note: #19 answers that 'assume bad actor' filters would have excluded a valid first report like the author's own. #21 also says most bad reports are valid, though not worth fixing.
claims.text: The majority of bounty submitters are adversarial to the bounty program, so bounty hunters must be assumed to be bad actors 99+% of the time.

claims.status_note: #21 argues nearly all bad reports are valid but not worth fixing, that community gatekeeping risks majority rule, and that most bugs go to private channels. #25 defines bad bugs but does not answer those points.
claims.text: Bad actors can be dealt with by exposing them and rallying a coinholder vote against them, with known facts posted on their thread.

claims.status_note: #20 likes the idea and objects only to auto-closing (c20). Nobody argues against automated pre-triage as such.
claims.text: An AI agent should run each reporter's PoC in a sandbox against the affected release before any human reviews it, since what matters is whether the exploit is confirmed, not whether a human or an agent submitted it.

claims.status_note: #20 warns tooling can fail and not every vulnerability fits a standard environment, and #22 adds that some attacks cannot be replicated immediately. The author of #19 does not reply.
claims.text: Reports whose PoC does not reproduce in the sandbox should be closed as spam, so no engineer time is spent on them.

claims.status_note: Nobody responds to the point or to the account of the disclosure.
claims.text: Filters that assume reporters are bad actors would have excluded aspiring newcomers; the author's valid first-ever High Zebra disclosure (GHSA-2p4c-3q4q-p463) came with no track record.

claims.status_note: #22 agrees ('Indeed') and adds theoretical attacks needing capital or time. Nobody disputes it.
claims.text: Automated validation should only prioritize, not reject: reproduced PoCs go to a priority queue and failures to a manual queue or back to the researcher, since tooling can fail and some attacks cannot be reproduced immediately.

claims.status_note: #25 says bad bugs also include non-bugs, AI hallucinations and made-up reports designed to game a payout. #21 does not reply.
claims.text: In 2026 nearly all 'bad' bug reports are technically valid but not worth fixing, and community gatekeeping of reports risks majority rule and misjudged severity.

claims.status_note: #24 replies with a different mechanism (c25) rather than arguing against it, and nobody else comments.
claims.text: Bounties should be offered for vulnerabilities, not bugs, by defining the impact types that matter and accepting only reports that fall into those categories.

claims.status_note: Nobody responds.
claims.text: A bug triaging platform should ingest bugs from trackers like GitHub, sort them, and let maintainers approve high-severity ones as legitimate vulnerabilities for optional evaluation, spreading the load bottom-up.

claims.status_note: #33 concludes any bounty program will be gamed and is wasted effort, without replying to #28 directly. The author of #28 does not return to the point.
claims.text: Having a bug bounty is a huge net positive: bounty hunters will spend LLM tokens, time and effort scrutinizing the code, raising the odds a vulnerability is found before attackers such as North Korean groups, who would attack regardless.

claims.status_note: Nobody responds.
claims.text: Awarding circuit soundness bugs has to rest with only a few trusted people, because nothing prevents someone from exploiting a flaw and then reporting it, and an anonymous reporter's honesty cannot be verified.

claims.status_note: Nobody responds.
claims.text: Reputation plus staged triage should filter slop first, with bonds applying only after repeated low-signal submissions; the real challenge is measuring confidence without discouraging odd but valid bugs.

claims.status_note: #33 replies about coinholder payouts but does not address whether researchers are still reporting.
claims.text: Researchers have kept reporting Zebra vulnerabilities since the bounty program ended, probably expecting their findings could earn a bounty.

claims.status_note: #33 independently confirms what #32 reports. Neither links the vote, and nobody disputes it.
claims.text: Coinholders have paid requested bounties for truly critical bugs, through the Q3 coinholder vote, at value-adjusted amounts.

mind_changes.note: thowar2 moves away from the bond-based bounty in #1 after replies; he does not name them, and #2 and #8 are the replies arguing against the bond and for paid reviewers.
mind_changes.span: I’m starting to be convinced by the replies that a bounty program may not be good idea and funds would just be better spent on hiring full time bug hunters instead of on reviewers.

posts.annotation: Proposes a bond for vulnerability reports so rejected slop costs money while confident reporters take the risk; says AI floods bounties with spam and CHG receives such requests; asks how it could go wrong.

Calls the bond the worst strategy: entry fees gatekeep bounties (Aave's $100 Sherlock fee, the Kelp DAO hack); proposes a full-time reviewer at about $100,000 a year; the pros of reporting must beat the cons.

Suggests Retroactive Grant guard rails: no projects already declined by ZCG or FPF, no bug bounties unless network-breaking like the Orchard bug; a real bounty program needs separate funding and qualified reviewers.

Says Taylor Hornby is a bad example: a bounty on top of a paid audit differs from a real bug bounty and is acceptable only as a voluntary grant; asks for the views of actual bounty hunters such as sangsoo.

Says ZF and ZCG reviewers were effectively DDOSed, a bond opens doors to real reviewers, and the default is no bounty; says strahncryptography's earlier public report was irresponsibly disclosed and not exploitable.

signals.note: Dismisses the preceding argument by pointing to the author's earlier public report and calling the response the work of the type of auditor to be disincentivized, rather than answering its points.
signals.span: So this response is coming from exactly the type of “auditor” we would want to disincentivize.

posts.annotation: Says coinholder votes should never be restricted by rules, only by norms, since they exist to override exceptions; calls the Taylor Hornby report a deserving example with no funding precedent yet.

Says his reported issue was fully exploitable and patched (links an issue), he never claimed to be an auditor, and the earlier reviewers were ordinary engineers with other duties, not dedicated triagers.

signals.note: Sarcastic opening aimed at the previous poster's remarks about him.
Corrects the claim in #5 that the report was not exploitable and links an issue where it can be checked.
signals.span: No, only one of the two was not practical, and the other was fully exploitable as well as patched: https://github.com/valargroup/vote-nullifier-pir/issues/118

posts.annotation: Opposes a large bond as a barrier for independent researchers; proposes several part- or full-time contract reviewers across expertise areas, recruited through an application form.

Says he is being convinced a bounty program may not be a good idea; funds are better spent on full-time bug hunters than reviewers; coinholders could vote discretionary bonuses for existential bugs, with no guaranteed bounty.

signals.note: States that the replies are moving him away from the bond-based bounty proposal in #1.
signals.span: I’m starting to be convinced by the replies that a bounty program may not be good idea and funds would just be better spent on hiring full time bug hunters instead of on reviewers.

posts.annotation: Supports Shawn's guard rails, citing a project whose grant ZCG stopped but which kept working and now seeks coinholder funds; says coinholder votes matter and a way to shun bad actors is needed.
Sees no reason to submit a bug bounty to ZCG, and says a bug found outside a ZCG grant would qualify on its own; agrees Retroactive Grants is not the place for it.
Says many security researchers besides Taylor caught critical bugs that prevented issues like double spends and chain halts.

Notes platforms like Immunefi use spam filtering, PoC requirements, AI triage and a 1 USDC fee; GHSA reports likely overwhelmed engineers lacking a dedicated triager; offers two options: a platform or a dedicated triager.
Strongly discourages bounty platforms: their terms conflict with Zcash's philosophy of shielded ZEC payouts, are often exclusionary, and may bring legal battles and law-enforcement requests.
Agrees other researchers found critical bugs but says Taylor illustrates a sorting problem between existential bugs and spam; asks how to judge bugs in between and which bounties CHG should cover.
Says the platform terms problem is another argument for having no bounty program at all.

Finds Immunefi appealing but its 1 USDC fee too low; says spammers drown out useful reports through an asymmetric economic attack; says most bounty submitters are adversarial, so bounty hunters must be assumed bad actors 99+% of the time.

signals.note: Ascribes bad faith to the whole group of bounty hunters, assuming it as the default.
signals.span: the majority of bounty submitters are adversarial to the bounty program, so 99+% of the time we have to assume that bounty hunters are bad actors.

posts.annotation: Says bad actors are handled by exposing them and rallying a vote against them, and asks readers to post known facts on the bad actor's thread.

Describes his own valid first disclosure (a High Zebra advisory), warns that 'assume bad actor' filters would exclude newcomers, and proposes an AI agent running each PoC in a sandbox so only reproducing reports reach engineers.

signals.note: The author discloses that he is a reporter whose Zebra disclosure would have earned a $75k award under the closed bounty program.
signals.span: GHSA-2p4c-3q4q-p463 (rated High) in Zebra was my first security disclosure ever, fixed in 6.2.1 and [credited in the 6.3.0 release](https://zfnd.org/zebra-6-3-0-release/). This would've been a $75k award under the now-closed ZCG bounty program.

posts.annotation: Likes automated PoC pre-triage but objects to closing non-reproducing reports as spam; proposes a priority queue for reproduced PoCs and a manual queue or request for more evidence for the rest.

signals.note: Endorses the goal of the proposal in #19 before raising an objection to its auto-closing step.
signals.span: I like the idea of having an automated pre-triage step that checks whether a PoC actually reproduces before sending the report to a human reviewer.

posts.annotation: Says most 'bad' reports in 2026 are actually valid but not worth fixing, so there is nothing to rally against; community gatekeeping risks majority rule and downplayed severity; asks how exposure would work for private reports.
Agrees automated reproduction misses theoretical attacks needing capital or time; restates his position: hire a full-time triager, not a platform, not bug hunters, not reliance on CG.
Says Zcash should offer bounties for vulnerabilities, not bugs, with defined impact categories and only reports in those categories accepted.
Proposes a triage platform that ingests bugs, lets maintainers approve high-severity ones as vulnerabilities for optional evaluation, and works bottom-up to reduce central load.
Defines bad bugs as non-bugs, hallucinations and fabricated reports; says flooding is an asymmetric economic attack no system survives, so the economics must change or there should be no bounty.

Says it is not an economic attack since nobody is paid before maintainers endorse a bug, as in 99.9% of programs; HackerOne hires full-time triagers, so hire an experienced one who can use AI for preliminary triage.
Links an exploited protocol that ran no bounty program and is now negotiating through one, calling it sad and saying we have to learn from this.

Says attackers such as North Korean groups would exploit regardless, but a bounty is a huge net positive since hunters spend LLM tokens and effort scrutinizing code, finding vulnerabilities before attackers do.

Says slop will be a problem; proposes a registration fee to self-fund and low rewards for non-critical bugs; circuit soundness awards must rest with few trusted people since a random could exploit then report.
Cites Solana's Alpenglow timed bounty: no platform, a burned 0.5 SOL fee per submission, SOL rewards up to 50K SOL, about 300 submissions; a designated person should handle triage.

Worries a bond prices out good-faith researchers; suggests reputation and staged triage to filter slop first, with bonds only after repeated low-signal submissions; confidence is hard to measure without discouraging odd valid bugs.

Notes researchers keep reporting Zebra vulnerabilities after the bounty ended, possibly expecting rewards given Q3 coinholder payouts for critical bugs, and asks how security reports should be handled.

After the discussion, believes any bounty program will be gamed endlessly and is wasted effort; coinholders have shown they pay for truly critical bugs, so discretionary payouts with no entitlement suffice.

open_questions.text: How should bugs between the obvious existential case and spam be judged as worthy of a bounty?
Which body should fund and review bounties: ZCG, Coinholder Grants, or a separate system with set-aside funding and dedicated reviewers?
Can a bond or fee deter slop without pricing out good-faith researchers?
Is mass submission an asymmetric economic attack, or is it manageable when nobody is paid before maintainers endorse a bug and a triager is hired?
How should Zcash handle security reports going forward, given researchers keep reporting Zebra bugs after the bounty ended?

overview.text: thowar2 opens by describing AI-driven slop reports that overwhelmed the earlier bounty program and now reach Coinholder Grants, and proposes a bond for submissions. strahncryptography calls it the worst strategy, argues bounties should not be gatekept, and wants a full-time reviewer; he also says Taylor Hornby is a poor example. Shawn suggests guard rails for Retroactive Grants, which thowar2 says coinholder votes should never be bound by.

thowar2 replies that ZF and ZCG reviewers were already DDOSed and points to a public report by strahncryptography as the sort of submission to disincentivize. strahncryptography answers with sarcasm and a link showing one of his two reports was exploitable and patched, and says the earlier reviewers were not dedicated triagers.

valens also opposes a large bond and proposes reviewers on retainer. thowar2 says he is starting to be convinced a bounty program may not be a good idea (#9). sangsoo offers a platform or a dedicated triager; strahncryptography opposes platforms and thowar2 calls that another argument against any bounty.

craftsoldier, a reporter, proposes sandboxed PoC checks to pre-triage reports and warns against bad-actor filters; valens objects to auto-closing and strahncryptography says some attacks cannot be replicated. strahncryptography and thowar2 disagree whether flooding is an economic attack, while sangsoo and strahncryptography offer a vulnerability-only scope and a triage platform.

Later posters add views: sangsoo calls a bounty a huge net positive, scalar suggests a registration fee, 0xKlastor cites Solana's burned-fee bounty with about 300 submissions, and operational-anxiety4 proposes reputation and staged triage.

Months later sangsoo notes researchers still report Zebra bugs and asks how reports should be handled. thowar2 says any bounty program will be gamed and wasted, but coinholders have shown they will pay for truly critical bugs, so discretionary payouts suffice.

positions.label: Make submitters post a bond or fee to deter slop
positions.summary: A cost to submit, forfeited on rejection, lifts the price of slop above its payoff while confident reporters accept it; forfeited bonds can fund reviewers, a registration fee can make the system self-funded, and Solana's burned fee drew only about 300 submissions.

positions.label: Keep reporting free and fund dedicated triagers
positions.summary: A bond gatekeeps a bounty whose impact falls on everyone and deters independent researchers. Paid triagers or reviewers, not engineers with other duties, should do the work.

positions.label: A bounty platform such as Immunefi could carry the load
positions.summary: Major projects use platforms with spam filtering, PoC requirements, AI triage and a 1 USDC fee; a sustainable program can use one or hire a dedicated triager.

positions.label: Bounty platforms conflict with Zcash and should be avoided
positions.summary: Platform terms of service conflict with Zcash's philosophy of shielded ZEC payouts, are often exclusionary, and risk legal battles and law-enforcement requests.

positions.label: No bounty program; pay truly critical bugs by coinholder vote
positions.summary: Any bounty program will be gamed endlessly and wastes administrative effort. Coinholders vote discretionary bonuses for truly existential bugs, with no entitlement, and reject most requests.

positions.label: Keep bounties out of Retroactive Grants
positions.summary: Retroactive Grants should exclude projects already declined by ZCG or FPF and bug bounties unless network-breaking; a real program needs separate funding and qualified reviewers.

positions.label: Coinholder votes should not be bound by rules
positions.summary: Restrictions on coinholder votes are neither possible nor desirable, because the votes exist to correct errors and override exceptions; norms are fine.

positions.label: Taylor Hornby's report is the model finding to reward
positions.summary: His report was an existential finding with clear consensus that it needed urgent fixing, so it shows what a bounty should reward.

positions.label: Taylor Hornby is not a representative bounty finder
positions.summary: He reported as a paid auditor and board member; a grant on top of an audit fee is not a tiered, contractual bounty, and the views of actual bounty hunters matter more.

positions.label: Run reporters' PoCs automatically before human review
positions.summary: A sandboxed AI agent runs each PoC against the affected release so engineers see only reproducing reports; valens would prioritize rather than auto-close failures.

positions.label: A bounty is a net positive for security
positions.summary: Bounty hunters will spend heavily on scrutinizing the code, and more eyes raise the chance a flaw is found before attackers find it, who would attack regardless.

positions.label: Sort reports by impact, reputation or maintainer approval
positions.summary: Offer bounties for vulnerabilities in defined impact categories, use a triage platform where maintainers approve high-severity bugs, or use reputation and staged triage with bonds only after repeated low-signal submissions.

summary.tldr: Thread on how Zcash should handle bug bounties now that AI makes slop reports cheap. The opening bond proposal drew objections that it gatekeeps researchers; dedicated triagers, PoC automation and platforms were debated, and the poster ended opposed to any formal bounty.
